speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting myself and other members of the house. Yesterday I was informed that an answer had been given to a question I had placed on the order paper concerning Canadian prisoners of war. The question was in two parts. The first dealt with numbers and the second with the total man days Canadians had been detained.
The answer to the first part was complete, but the information I asked for in the second part was denied, the statement being made that this information could be obtained only by a review of each of the files of the 9,552 prisoners of war. Representations have been made to me and to other members of the house that Canadian prisoners of war be paid one dollar for each day of their internment, similar to the amount that it is claimed was paid in the United States. Without knowledge as to the total number of man days Canadians were detained, it is impossible to assess how practical this suggestion is. Therefore I would request that the question be replaced on the order paper, and that I be given the information I desire.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are proceeded with I should like to give to the house an indication of the measures it is expected that the house will be asked to consider during the present session in addition to those already on the order paper. Hon. members will recall that this information was asked for some days ago by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) mentioned it again on Wednesday.
There will of course be the budget legislation, the appropriation bill, and the usual measure respecting the financing of Canadian National Railways. The Minister of Finance also plans to introduce amendments to the following statutes: Foreign Insurance Companies Act; Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act; Tariff Board Act; Trust Companies Act; Loan Companies Act. I understand that all these amendments are of a minor nature to facilitate the administration of the statutes.
It is expected that there will be legislation to revise the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act and to implement the tax agreement with France.
The Minister of Agriculture plans to introduce a measure respecting the Cold Storage Act. This is merely to repeal part II of the act, which has never been applied, and for the purposes of which there is now other legislation which is being used.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will have a bill to revise the Indian Act, and may also have an amendment to the Canadian Citizenship Act. The Minister of Justice may introduce an amendment to the Official Secrets Act, and a statute law amendment bill respecting proceedings by and against crown corporations, to facilitate the recourse of individuals against such corporations.
The Minister of National Revenue plans to bring in an amendment to the Customs Act. The Postmaster General expects to have an amendment to the Post Office Act.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce plans to present a bill respecting defence purchasing, as well as amendments to the following statutes: Canada Grain Act; Gas Inspection Act; Electricity Inspection Act.
The Minister of Transport has an amendment to the Canada Shipping Act, which has been referred to already in debate. In addition to legislation, it is expected that there will be resolutions to approve the international convention on northwest Atlantic fisheries and the world meteorological convention.
Various departments are giving consideration and have been giving consideration for some time to certain other measures, and it is possible that some of these may be introduced and given first reading so that they may be available for consideration by hon. members and the public during the parliamentary recess. It is not expected that there will be any desire to have them enacted into legislation at this session. It has frequently been found to be satisfactory to members of the public who are interested to have bills read the first time and distributed so that in the recess they may receive consideration and representations may be made in connection therewith.
While I am not in the confidence of my colleagues with respect to it, I understand that there may be a bill respecting a residence for the Prime Minister.
Hon. members will realize that unforeseen circumstances or developments may require parliament to consider some additional matters^ but that does not appear to be likely. I think what I have indicated, together with what we have on the order paper, will complete the list of matters to which we shall be inviting consideration at this session.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the tone of the representations made by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), and the spirit in which he made them. Nevertheless it is our understanding that the Indians are anxious to have this legislation brought before parliament. This matter has been discussed. The department felt it had all the information required for the drafting of the legislation, and that it would be desirable that the bill be given first reading and be distributed, and then that a sufficient lapse of time be allowed so that interested chiefs and other members of their bands may see what it contains and make representations. If it appeared from their reaction to the bill that they would prefer not to have it adopted at this session but rather to have further discussions with them and further consideration of the legislation, their views would be given sympathetic consideration.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL GRANT TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Railway Act to increase the annual grant to the grade crossing fund from $500,000 to $1,000,000 for six consecutive years from April 1, 1951.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL GRANT TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Will the minister make a statement, please?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL GRANT TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the object of the resolution is to increase from $500,000 to $1 million the amount which may be paid into the grade crossing fund. There will also be a provision to increase the payment which may be made in the case of any one project from $100,000 to $150,000.
I think it might be useful to the house if I were to give a short historical analysis of the grade crossing fund and the various changes, whether by way of amendment or otherwise, which have taken place from time to time.

The fund was established in 1909 by 8-9 Edward VII, chapter 32, section 7, which appropriated and placed to the credit of the fund $200,000 per annum for five years from April 1, 1909. Under this statute not more than twenty per cent of the cost of construction work could be paid out of the fund.
In 1914 the annual grants of $200,000 were extended for five more years. In 1919 those grants were extended for ten years from April 1, 1919, and it was provided that not more than twenty-five per cent of the cost of construction work could be paid out of the fund, with a further provision that not more than $15,000 could be paid in the case of any one crossing or for any one project. In 1926 the act was further amended to provide that the amount payable out of the fund in the case of any one crossing should not exceed forty per cent of the total cost, and should not in any case exceed $25,000. In 1928 the limit was increased to $100,000. In 1929 the annual grants of $200,000 were extended for ten years from April 1, 1929.
Between 1934 and 1939 additional amounts were credited to the fund under various statutes. No additions were made to the fund between April 1, 1939, and April 1, 1947, but by chapter 70 of the statutes of 1947 the fund was to be credited with $200,000 per annum for ten years from April 1, 1947. Again, by chapter 27 of the statutes of 1948, the annual amount to be credited to the fund for the nine years commencing April 1,	1948, was
increased to $500,000.
As I have stated, this legislation will increase the annual grant for a period of six years to $1 million, beginning April 1, 1951. The house might like to have on record the amounts paid out of the fund over the last few years, which have been as follows:

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL GRANT TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the railway grade crossing fund is always an interesting subject of discussion. In his review of the history of the fund the minister has indicated that the present resolution contemplates two broad purposes, the first being to increase the annual statutory amount available from $500,000 to $1 million per annum for the six years from April 1, 1951, and the second to permit $150,000 instead of the previous limit of $100,000 to be used for any one particular work coming within the scope of the act.
I do not propose to review the history of this legislation, except to say very briefly that these provisions, which are embodied in section 262 of the Railway Act, have been most beneficial in their operation during the forty-one years they have been in effect. The amounts made available under the statute, of course, do not represent all the money that has been paid into the railway grade crossing fund and made available for crossing protection. During the days of the depression, particularly, large sums of money were made available by parliament to supplement the annual statutory grant, which at that time was $200,000.
Hon. members will realize that during the forty-one years the railway grade crossing fund has been in existence a substantial total amount of money has been made available by parliament. The annual report of the Department of Transport for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1949, shows that total authorizations from 1909 to 1949 amounted to $14,062,000 odd. Certain of those authoriza-; tions lapsed, but total expenditures to March 31, 1949, were just under $12 million.
Hon. members will also realize, of course, that this does not represent the entire amount that has been expended on grade separation during this period. That total of some $12 million simply represents the contribution made by parliament toward the cost of grade separation and crossing protection works, under the direction of the

Railway Act
board of transport commissioners. The minister has not given the total amount spent for this purpose, though he did so when the 1948 amendment was before the house. While I have not seen the latest figures I think they probably amount now to something like $50 million which has been spent in this period of time on grade separation works, which includes the contribution of $12 million from the railway grade crossing fund.
The uses to which the fund has been put in these years have been uniform. The fund has always been designated by parliament, and is still designated, as being for the following purpose: to aid actual construction work for the protection, safety and convenience of the public in respect of highway crossings of railways at rail level in accordance with the provisions of section 262 of the Railway Act. I infer from the statement the minister has made today that no enlargement of or changes in the scope of those purposes are intended.
On the subject of the limit on individual grants, sir, it is quite clear, from a review of this legislation in the forty-one year period it has been on the statute book, that the practice of parliament has been from time to time to increase both the percentage and the total amount which may be ordered by the board of transport commissioners to be contributed out of the railway grade crossing fund to the cost of any crossing protection. This has been a uniform development throughout the period. The direction of the change has always been upward, both as to percentage and total amount. It is interesting to hear the minister indicate that one of the purposes of the bill is to increase, not the percentage, but the total amount for any one work from $100,000 to $150,000, for the ample reasons which the minister has given.
In indicating the reasons why this measure should be entitled to support, I should like to say briefly that there are some factors that are readily apparent. When the railway grade crossing fund was first established, it was intended to assist in meeting principally the problem of maintaining public safety; that is the paramount consideration in the application of these moneys. On the other hand, there are additional considerations, such as the question of public convenience, more expeditious transportation on the part of both the railways and those using the highways, and, to some extent, employment. These have been factors worthy of consideration.
The report of the board of transport commissioners for the year ended December 31, 1948-the report for the calendar year 1949 is not available in printed form as yet- indicates not merely what has been the trend of accidents at level crossings in the past,

but also how the accidents have been influenced by the type of crossing protection available at these highway crossings. At page 97 of the report we have the figures for the ten-year period 1939-1948 showing that at crossings of highways and railways in this period there have been 3,541 accidents, in which 1,342 people were killed and 5,024 people were injured. The year 1947 had the highest accident record in the ten-year period. In that year there were 638 persons injured and 162 killed in 442 accidents.
Let us just translate those statistics into other figures. It means that every day of the year there was an average of more than one accident at a railway crossing. In the year 1948 there were 414 such accidents, with 159 persons killed and 566 injured.
A further table on the same page of the report of the board of transport commissioners indicates how those accidents in the year 1948 were related to the type of protection existing at the crossings where the accidents occurred. I mentioned that there were 414 accidents in that year. This is how the statistics are broken down in the report: Number of accidents which occurred at crossings protected by gates, 8; number of accidents which occurred at crossings protected by automatic highway traffic signals, one; number of accidents which occurred at crossings protected by bell, 6; number of accidents which occurred at crossings protected by bell and wigwag, 40; number of accidents which occurred at crossings protected by flashing light signals and bells, 10; number of accidents which occurred at crossings protected by watchmen, 7; number of accidents which occurred at crossings unprotected, 342.
It will thus be seen that of those 414 accidents in the year 1948 over eighty per cent of them occurred at unprotected crossings. I submit, sir, that is a fact of great significance in our approach to this problem, and the question presented to us whether the house should authorize an increase from $500,000 to $1 million per annum in the fund.
I am sure hon. members of this house are going to approach this question from two points of view. Not the less important or less urgent of the two is the humane consideration. The fact that we have, as revealed in the figures I have just read, a record of death, maiming and tragedy to many families in this country, will give every member of the house cause for deep regret, and a desire to do what may reasonably lie within the power of parliament to meet the needs of the situation. I am sure I do not need to dwell on that aspect of the problem.

Because the problem has economic aspects as well, sir, I mention these briefly. As I understand them, every one of these economic factors favours the increase in the proposed statutory appropriation. As the minister mentioned, there is, first, the increased cost of crossing protection works, and that has been a factor of great importance. The limitation that has existed of $100,000 has meant that the fund has not been available to carry the full share that might well be expected of it when works of major importance and high cost have been directed by the board of transport commissioners.
The second aspect, sir, is the plight of the railways. The railways are faced with serious financial problems. I am not going to discuss any questions that are now engaging the attention of the royal commission on transportation, or have been engaging the attention of the board of transport commissioners. I do say that the railways are faced with serious financial problems, and they are not in a position to undertake the cost of a program of crossing protection in this country on any substantial scale.
A third factor, sir, and it is one to which importance must be attached, is the fact that throughout the years there has been an increased tendency, recognized in the legislation, for the public represented by parliament, to participate in meeting the costs of these grade separation works. Mention has already been made of the way in which the percentage and amount available out of the fund for any particular work have been increased by legislation. It is a fact that the invariable tendency of legislation pertaining to the fund since its inception has been to increase provision for public contribution to the cost of grade separation works. Indeed, even within the limits created by parliament, the board of transport commissioners, in awarding sums out of the grade separation fund toward the cost of crossing protection, has applied a similar tendency on its own part. In a decision of the board in 1928, the case of Toronto
v.	C.P.R. and C.N.R., reported in 34 Canadian Railway Cases at page 143, the board recognized that tendency in these words:
The tendency, on the whole,-
That is to say, the tendency within the jurisprudence of the board in relation to awards out of the fund.
-has been to increase the percentage contribution which the city or municipality is required to make.
That is to say, the portion that the public has been called upon to contribute by reason of the public use of these crossings.
The fourth factor is the great and extensive highway improvement program undertaken by most, if not all, of the provinces.
Railway Act
This highway improvement and extension program is a factor that is going to have a direct bearing upon the question of crossing protection.
A fifth factor is the heavy increase in highway traffic. I have obtained some statistics on this subject, but the statistics for 1949 are not yet available. Anyone who has made a study of the increase in highway traffic will not fail to have been profoundly impressed by the tremendous increases that have occurred during the period of the life of the railway grade crossing fund.
The earliest figures on the numbers of motor vehicles registered in Canada go back to 1904, when there were 535 registered. In 1909, the year when the railway grade crossing fund came into existence, there were 4,809 motor vehicles registered in Canada. Every year, with scarcely any pause, save in several of the depression years, there has been a steady increase in the number of motor vehicles registered in Canada. I mention the figures for only a few of the years. In 1915 there were 95,284; in 1920, 408,790; in 1925, 724,048. The million mark was passed in the year 1928. In 1935 there were 1,176,000. In 1940 the 1,500,000 mark was passed. In 1948 the number of motor vehicles registered in Canada had passed the two million mark. The figure for that year is 2,035,352.
Parliament must have regard to that stupendous increase, during the relatively short period of time to which I have referred, in the number of motor vehicles using our highways in all the provinces, and in the number of vehicles that are daily crossing railways at grade.
A sixth factor that might be mentioned is the higher speed of motor vehicles today. The higher speed of motor vehicles has unquestionably been a factor in the accident toll at grade crossings; and the fact stares us in the face that more powerful motorcars are being turned out all the time, and that the degree of care exercised by drivers has not always kept pace with the increase in the power of the motorcars under their control.
Then there is one additional factor, although it has not always been as potent a factor as it was during the depression years when parliament was voting additional moneys for the purpose of providing employment while proceeding with the beneficial work of eliminating crossings. It is a fact that at different times during the depression years the fund was exhausted because so many grade separation schemes or crossing protection schemes were undertaken, and there was not always enough money in the fund to meet the demand. There are in Canada, more particularly in certain areas,

Railway Act
problems of unemployment to which beneficial works carried on with the assistance of the railway grade crossing fund can help to contribute a solution.
In conclusion, therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say that the house must recognize the need for increasing the sums provided at the public expense to contribute toward these works of grade separation and crossing protection which are of general public benefit. We have a bigger problem in this respect today than we had in the past. The bigger problem justifies an increase in the funds voted by parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to express support of the legislation anticipated by this resolution. My only regret is that it does not 50 a bit further.
It so happens that the constituency I represent, Winnipeg North Centre, has the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway cut into it at the eastern end; and then that railway line, after forming the northern boundary of the constituency for most of its length, bisects it again at the western end. In other words, there are grade crossings in Elmwood at the eastern end of my riding, and in Brooklands at the western end.
I make reference to that fact because I think it serves to justify the principle which is at the heart of this grade crossing legislation, namely that the cost of these grade separation projects is a cost that should not be borne to any extent, if at all, by the local people. After all, the line of the railway to which I have referred is the main line of the Canadian Pacific running from Montreal to Vancouver. Since that line serves the whole of Canada, and since its revenues are derived from all over Canada in part because it is able to go through the two communities that I have named, surely it should not fall upon those communities to protect themselves against the hazards of grade crossings in those areas.
It seems to me there is no doubt as to the justification for this principle, namely, that at least a good-sized portion of the cost of the grade crossings should be paid for out of the general revenues of the nation rather than that that cost should be imposed upon the local people. In fact, when I think of a community such as Brooklands, at the west end of Winnipeg, or a community such as Elmwood, which, although it is part of Winnipeg, is at the east end of the city and is in a sense a community by itself, I cannot see any fairness in their having to pay anything at all towards the elimination of grade crossings on the main transcontinental line of the Canadian Pacific railway. So I earnestly

hope that as time goes on it will be recognized that the cost of eliminating the hazards of level crossings in such areas should be borne, I would say, by two authorities, namely, the federal government and the railway concerned.
As it now stands, a community such as Brooklands could apply for the elimination of one or two grade crossings where the Canadian Pacific railway passes through the village. But the public finances of that particular community are limited, and they know it would be useless to apply, because, if the application were granted, in the end a portion of the cost would be assessed back to them by the board of transport commissioners. This makes it completely prohibitive so far as that community is concerned.
Elmwood is not in a.much better position, because, although it forms part of the city of Winnipeg, and it would be the city that would have to make the application and therefore bear part of the cost, when the people of Elmwood go before the city council in Winnipeg they find themselves confronted with the fact that they are just one community at one end of the city. The city must think twice before taking money out of the city treasury to remedy a condition at one corner of the city, when they also have in mind the factor I have already indicated, namely, that the need for the grade separation in question arises because a transcontinental railway happens to go through that area.
The minister knows that from time to time I have raised the question of the grade crossings in the areas to which I have just referred, and have expressed the hope almost every year that necessary changes would be made in the legislation so that these particular grade crossings might be eliminated.
I am sure when I refer to Elmwood and Brooklands in Manitoba I am citing cases which are but typical of many like unto them throughout the country. There must be many a municipality, through which a main line or even a branch line of a railway passes, which cannot afford the money it would have to pay-the share of the cost that would be assessed against it-if it did make application to the board of transport commissioners for a grade separation and such application were granted. Yet in these cases the hazards are such that the grade crossings should be eliminated.
I must also express disappointment in the fact that the hope the minister held out to me a couple of years ago seems to have been put on the shelf-and I use that figure of speech advisedly. As late as April 20, 1948, as it is recorded at page 3167 of Hansard, the

Railway Act
My point is that in places where there is heavy traffic it would seem to be common sense and perhaps economical in the end if the traffic were stopped only when trains were in the vicinity instead of requiring everybody to stop every time they come to a railroad crossing.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the house will expect some information with reference to the reasons why the department has seen fit to propose this bill to the house. I gave certain information when we had first reading of the bill, and I think that additional reasons should now be given for the proposed measure. The Department of Transport Stores Act was enacted in 1937 following the formation of the Department of Transport in November, 1936. There were at that time sixty stores depots scattered over Canada from coast to coast with as many as three, and in one instance four, in one city. There were also at that time ten separate votes in the department carrying their own stocks in a total of sixty stores depots. In the stores depots there were five or six separate compartments, and goods purchased under one

Department of Transport Stores appropriation were placed in one compartment and could not quickly be transferred to another compartment where the same stores were required. Now there is a consolidated account to meet stores requirements of fifty votes through thirty stores depots.
The purpose of the act was to enable the department to consolidate stores and stores depots, and to provide a centralized purchasing control over stores. To simplify the control and use of the stores the act provided for a single account called "Department of Transport stores account". This is the controlling account to which all stores are charged when purchased and to which all issues are credited.
In order to give the department working capital to be used for the purchase of stores in advance of appropriations voted by parliament the act authorized the Minister of Finance to advance to the Minister of Transport out of the consolidated revenue fund up to $1 million. This operates as a revolving fund. When the stores are issued for use in the various services such as lighthouse service, dominion steamers, air services, canals, etc., the value of such stores is charged to the proper appropriation and the revolving fund is credited with that amount. The fund is like the water in a well out of which the stores are drawn and which is fed by the appropriations. When stores are drawn the level of the water in the well is lowered but is restored again to its former level by new credits drawn from the appropriations.
There was a precedent for this fund in the Public Printing and Stationery Act amendment contained in chapter 5 of the statutes of 1928. Advances up to $700,000 were authorized to be made out of the consolidated fund to the king's printer to enable him to purchase materials and pay wages. This fund was subsequently increased to $2 million in 1946.
Section 6 of the Department of Transport Stores Act provided that the inventory of stores at the end of each fiscal year should not exceed the amount of stores inventory established as of April 1, 1937, which was $957,000. In 1939 the act was amended to increase this inventory ceiling to $1,250,000, and again in 1946 the inventory ceiling was further increased to $1,600,000. It is now considered that there should be no inventory ceiling at all and that it was a mistake to have one in the first place. The Right Hon. R. B. Bennett observed on second reading of the 1937 bill, as recorded at page 2488 of Hansard for that year, that it was a peremptory statement to put in a statute that the inventory must be reduced to the fixed limit,

and that if in the course of business the minister did not find it possible to reduce the inventory he is confronted by a statute that says he must do it. The difficulty is that the officers of the department cannot foretell prior to March 31 what the inventory will be at that date, which would enable corrective action to be taken at the proper time. In commercial business a merchant can put on a sale to reduce inventory but the department cannot do this, and it cannot issue stores unless they are required. The tendency has been for the stores inventory to increase owing to increased prices and additional requirements in Newfoundland and elsewhere, and now it is far above the statutory limit, being estimated at $3,200,000 as at March 31, 1950. There is no machinery for reducing inventory except to stop buying and to issue out the stock on hand.
It is submitted that the proper control over the size of the inventory is found in the amount of money which is authorized to be spent on the purchase of stores and by a careful scrutiny of purchase orders before the same are placed. If hon. members will look at the bill they will see that there are four pertinent amendments.
1.	It is proposed to increase the amount
of the advances authorized under section 3 of the act as working capital from $1 million to $5 million. This is required for the following reasons:	(a) Price increases. The $1
million will not go half as far as it did in 1939.
(b)	Taking over Newfoundland stores estimated at $1,180,000.

If larger inventories must be held than the value of $1,600,000, then the minister should name the figure and put it in the act. Instead of that he is asking for a provision which means, in effect, that the sky is the limit on the value of stores that can be held in stock.
That point was dealt with in the debate in 1937, and the present Minister of Trade and Commerce referred several times to the fact that there was no need for a larger amount. At page 2486 of Hansard of April 2, 1937, he said:
Our annual purchases of stores are about $3 million and our stocks today are $1,500,000, which of course is an absurd figure. I have gone into the matter in an effort to have the stocks reduced and it has been explained to me that it is impossible to reduce them without legislation of this sort so that they may be combined for the various services.
As I said a few minutes ago, the minister said at page 2488 of the same volume:
It will be my aim to see that at the end of the year there are no surplus stocks.
I do suggest that under these conditions the minister and his department are asking too much. There should be a lower figure set for the revolving fund, and a limit on the value of those stores which can be held by the department should be maintained. If this proposed amendment is carried, then we are just leaving the door open for extravagance and possible waste.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext:
No. I think we should give this matter a little further thought It is perfectly clear, when you read the speeches which were made at the outset, that this thing had turned out absolutely differently from what was expected. I therefore think we should have another good look at it now before we greatly extend the scope of it. I should like to read from Mr. Howe's speech when expanding the thing originally. This is to be found in Hansard of April 2, 1937, at page 2486.
I draw to your attention, Mr. Chairman, and to the minister's attention some of the things he said because I think, as has already been pointed out, that it is extremely easy to buy stores and to get them into stock and, I should think, extremely difficult to get the things cleared out. Incidentally, we shall not hold the minister too seriously accountable for having been a lawbreaker; of course, we are getting used to that sort of thing. Nevertheless, it does not encourage us to think that the thing is working excellently 

and then to learn that he has found it necessary to exceed by almost three times, if I remember aright, the amount he is supposed to carry. Let me read one or two things that were said, and I think we should consider them rather carefully because we are really plunging ahead further along a course which, I submit, up to the present, has proved to be not satisfactory. Mr. Howe said:
As I said on the first reading, this is to simplify the bookkeeping and handling of stores in the Department of Transport. We believe that inevitably it will reduce the inventory of stores which are now carried-[DOT]
And so on. Then he referred, as the minister has already done, to their having sixty store depots from coast to coast; and a little later on he said:
Our annual purchases of stores are about $3 million, and our stocks today are $1,500,000, which of course is an absurd figure. I have gone into the matter in an effort to have the stocks reduced and it has been explained to me that it is impossible to reduce them without legislation of this sort . . .
The reason for that apparently was that there were complicated relationships among the different stores, and a lot of complicated bookkeeping, and the minister wanted to set up this one fund which he said was going to simplify things. Then he goes on and refers to the dominion steamers and the lighthouse service, and the canals; now of course we have the airports.. Then Mr. Howe says this; I draw this particularly to the attention of the minister, and I think we should have some further information along this line before we go any further. Mr. Howe says further, as reported at page 2487:
The bill provides that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Transport shall agree upon an initial price. That is necessary because some of these stores go back fifty years though they are still carried at cost price.
One of the things I should like to have before we go further in this is some kind of pedigree of the stores we have now. I should like to know what we have now that is, say, ten, twenty or thirty years old. Maybe this clean-up has been made. On the other hand I should like to know how much we have relative to what is used from time to time, because I understand the Hoover commission found that in one department in the United States they had stocked themselves up for fifty years into the future. You get it both ways. You have old stuff up to fifty years of age and then you have enthusiasts going ahead and buying away into the future.
Having said that, I should like to recall to you, Mr. Chairman, what the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has already said about how inviting it is to permanent officials to have money to spend. We all like money to

spend, particularly if it is not our own money. I should like to get some kind of statement, not in exhaustive detail but nevertheless in a certain amount of detail, as to what is in there now.
There is another question I should like to ask the minister, and it is as to what extent the things that are in these stores are specialized things that cannot be bought elsewhere; in other words, which are not readily available through the ordinary channels of purchase. Have we got a lot of things in our stores which actually we could buy without delay in the ordinary course of merchandising? If that is so, why do we have these things? Because if we have them, it merely means that we are keeping up storehouses and paying people to look after them. These are things that occur to one offhand. I base them, to some extent, on the original expectation which was in the mind of the minister when this department was set up. I am just looking for another statement which Mr. Howe made. I have it now. Another thing Mr. Howe said was this:
Today the stocks are one and a half million. It will be my aim to see that at the end of the year there are no surplus stocks.
To what extent have those aims been carried out? To what extent have we got a lot of people who are in the business of keeping stores and who probably like to keep stores? To what extent have we got stock that is piling up and perhaps should be cleared out? To what extent are we buying things away in advance? And finally, to what extent are we storing up things that we could buy in the open market in any of the places where we actually have these stores at the present time?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member has asked some questions which I shall try to clear up. In the first place he would like to know what stores are on hand now. Of course, that is a little difficult to answer.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext: I admit I would not ask to get it down to the last detail.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext:
He was kind enough to say he would not insist too much upon a strict interpretation of the question. There are at the present time some thirty stores depots in the department, from coast to coast. There would be a stores depot in Quebec, one in Victoria, another in Vancouver, another at Charlottetown, and now one at Gander. There would be in those stores depots all sorts of consumable stores.
It is difficult to give a detailed explanation of what they would be. But when the hon. member asked what the specialized stores might be, I can think of those in the radio
Department of Transport Stores service, those in the air service and those in the marine service. For instance, in marine stores at Quebec there would be all sorts of things required for the dominion icebreaking fleet, and for the steamers which take supplies to lighthouse keepers. Those are stores of a specialized nature.
It would not be easy, I think, to give a breakdown of the total inventory of the stores, although it is possible to give the total amount which, as I indicated a moment ago, is $3,200,000.
Then the hon. member inquired about a statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to the effect that an attempt would be made to get rid of obsolescent stores. I am informed by my officers that all obsolescent stores were disposed of back in 1937, and there are in our depots no stores purchased prior to 1937. At least one, and perhaps two, sections of the bill deal with obsolescent stores, and the manner in which they should be disposed of. I hope the house will agree that these provisions are a considerable improvement over what we had before.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext: Does not the provision in section 8 make it easier to keep down the amount of stores on hand? My understanding of this new section is that it simplifies the procedure for getting rid of obsolescent stores. This means there would be fewer stores on hand, and that the ceiling could be that much lower.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext: It would not mean that there are fewer stores on hand, but it refers to the method by which obsolescent stores should be disposed of.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext: It makes it easier to dispose of them.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, quite. But I wonder if we should discuss it before reaching that section.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext: My understanding of the revolving fund is that it is required only for the purchase of goods needed before the appropriations are passed by the house; in other words, most of the purchases are covered by the appropriations put through the house. This revolving fund is merely to provide for goods that have to be kept in store, and that will be required before the appropriation can be put through?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext:
I would not like to say that it is or is not. I think on the whole the hon. member is correct, but I did not follow his question as closely as perhaps I should have. The revolving fund is required not only to purchase stocks between the time the fiscal

Department of Transport Stores year ends and the amount is voted in the next fiscal year, but it is also to keep on hand stocks required from time to time.
For instance, about this time of year great quantities of stocks are required for our steamship service in connection with the opening of navigation. If the storekeepers of the various depots waited until this time to make their purchases, the ships would be held up. So that during the course of the winter, and even before that, they stock up with those things likely to be required by icebreakers and by the dominion steamers which replenish the supplies required by lighthouse keepers, and the like. So that the revolving fund is required for the purposes mentioned by the hon. member, but also for other purposes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext: But 'most of those purchases would be made out of money appropriated by parliament last year.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext: To a large extent.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext:
We passed estimates last summer, or last fall, so that the Department of Transport could buy most of those requirements. That point was dealt with by Mr. Howe in 1939 when, as reported at page 2642 of Hansard, he said:
There are several departments that have revolving funds of that kind. For instance, the national harbours board is entitled to expend $1 million beyond its appropriation, with the understanding that this amount will be the first charge on the new appropriations. The printing bureau also has provision for a revolving fund, and I believe last year the Department of Mines and Resources set up a revolving fund for work among the Indians.
Will the minister tell us what other revolving funds there are at the present time? It looks as though this particular revolving fund of $5 million is the largest in the whole government service.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, it is; I understand it is the largest one. But the hon. member should not forget that the purchases of the Department of Transport, so far as stores are concerned, are perhaps the largest too.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext: Of course the bulk of these purchases would be made out of moneys appropriated at the preceding session.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext:
One does not wish to have a lot of information just for the sake of having information; but I do think we are proceeding blindly at the present time. I am groping in my mind as to what would be a reasonable and feasible request-and perhaps the minister could improve upon it -but I would like to have at least a sample. I suggest that he might give us that information in respect of the larger stores-and he may pick out whichever he chooses, whether it


be Montreal, Quebec, Toronto, or some other place. But we would like to have some idea as to the main categories of these stores, the value of them and, in particular, which of them are special things which could not be readily obtainable and would need to be kept in stock.
I suggest information of that kind should be given to us. I am quite ready to alter my requirements a little, if the minister would suggest something that would give me what I want, and which he would find easier to supply. I base these observations on the fact that this has turned out quite differently from what the minister had expected originally. While we are not labouring the point, he has told us that he has exceeded his authority-and I am sure he has done it in good faith, and has done it because he thought it was necessary.
As I say, however, I would like to have a cross section of these stores so that we may understand them. If the minister does not think that is the best way to give the information then, as I have said, I am quite ready to consider altering my question. We should have information of that kind; otherwise we are just becoming rubber stamps-which is not altogether unknown in this chamber.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext: I do not think I can add much to what I said before. There are thirty or thirty-two stores in the department, scattered from one end of the country to the other. These stores have to do with marine services, canal services, air services, and telegraph and telephone services. Those again are broken down into other groups. I do not know that I am called upon to give an inventory of the different depots, and I do not know that my hon. friend wants that. I have indicated to the committee that the stores on hand are over $3 million. The section we are now discussing seeks authority to increase them to $5 million. I have given the reason why the officers of the department feel that $3 million would not be sufficient and that $5 million is required. I have indicated also that finance in consultation with treasury and the Auditor General's staff thinks that this is not only necessary but peremptory.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister in his usual nice way is trying to get this thing along. But, after all, all that the minister has done is to give us some generalities. He has asked us to accept his judgment as to the situation; he has referred to the finance department and to the Auditor General, all of which is quite impressive. But surely what I am asking is perfectly feasible. I am asking for an inventory of the main classes, let us say, in one of the largest depots, so that we

may reach some conclusion and not merely be in the position we are so often asked to be in, of just accepting what the minister gives us.
The minister has given certain general reasons. I would point out to him that if we stick to general reasons I can go on and spend the rest of the afternoon quoting what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said. Evidently the minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have entirely different ideas as to how this should be done. I do not think it is unreasonable to ask for the figures in regard to one of the depots.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT WITH RESPECT TO OUTSTANDING ADVANCES, OBSOLETE STORES, ETC.
speechtext: I have not been present during all the time this bill has been before the committee, but I do not think it should be too difficult for the committee to have an understanding as to whether the minister is asking for too much. First of all, I think we ought to know the value of the stores bought and used during the year. Surely this plan of having a revolving fund should be' followed only in very rare instances. In 1939 the present Minister of Trade and Commerce instanced the printing bureau and the Department of Mines and Resources. It must be perfectly obvious to all hon. members that financing by means of a revolving fund is entirely out of line with our method of government financing, which should be carried on by means of


appropriations. It is only in very rare cases that a revolving fund should be required. The minister already has a revolving fund of $1 million. He has told the committee that last year he required a few thousand dollars over that figure, so a revolving fund of $2 million should be more than ample to meet the requirements of his department; and I suggest that even at that figure it will be higher than any other revolving fund in the government service.
The use of revolving funds strikes at the very root of the authority of parliament, which is supposed to have control of the purse strings. The theory is that nothing may be spent by any government until that money has been appropriated by parliament, and particularly by the House of Commons. The use of these revolving funds derogates from that power of the House of Commons. Here we have an instance in which the minister himself admits that he has not needed even $2 million in that fund. So I urge that he accept the amendment and let the figure stand at $2 million rather than ask for this amount of $5 million in the revolving fund.

I would ask, Mr. Chairman, that before this administration item is carried, the minister make a statement to the house about the present situation in shipbuilding and shipping. It is quite impossible for those of us who are responsible for dealing with the estimates to discuss these particular subjects

until we have a statement from the minister. For example, with regard to shipbuilding, there was a bill passed at the last session which provided for accelerated depreciation for shipyards under certain conditions. We should like to know from the minister what results have flowed from that legislation, whether there has been an increase in shipbuilding in Canada.
We should also like to know whether or not any of the funds which have been held in trust for ship owners, who sold their cargo vessels to a foreign flag company, have been used for the building of new ships. We all recognize the great importance of having modern fast cargo vessels for Canada, and it was the understanding that this money was to be held in escrow by the Canadian maritime commission, and would be used for the building of these new ships. We would like to know whether any ships have been built.
The government announced a new policy for the Canadian merchant marine at the close of the last session. Roughly speaking, the plan was to reduce the Canadian merchant fleet to forty vessels, all of which were to be eligible for a subsidy. I believe there was to be an amount provided in the estimates this year for that subsidy. The plan involved the transfer of a good many ships from Canadian registry to United Kingdom registry. It meant also that many Canadian ships would be laid up, or put in mothballs, and a great many Canadian seamen would lose their employment, or as they say, "go on the beach". I ask the minister to let us know before this administration item is passed just what the picture is with regard to both those questions; first, the question of shipbuilding in Canada, and second the Canadian shipping policy. We have had no definite information on either of them since the last session, and the committee is entitled to have the facts and figures showing just how those policies are working out. If we do not get that, it is quite impossible for us to deal with these questions.

And there will be a full opportunity for this house to debate the matter before any such change is made.
They are statutory rates, and could not be changed without an amendment to the statute.

There is one point I should like to have clarified at this time. Supply-Transport
Mr Chevrier: The Canadian National Railways items come under the Department of Transport.
What about Trans-Canada Air Lines?
Trans-Canada Air Lines come under the Department of Trade and Commerce.
How can that be, in view of the fact that Trans-Canada Air Lines is a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Canadian National Railways?
By virtue of the assignment of duties act, the Trans-Canada Air Lines have been assigned to the Minister of Trade and Commerce just as the C.B.C. has been given to the Minister of National Revenue.

I believe, Mr. Chairman, that this is the appropriate point at which to indicate the inconsistency of this situation. The Trans-Canada Air Lines is, in fact, a part of the Canadian National Railways, no matter what may be said to the contrary. The Canadian National Railways entirely own the Trans-Canada Air Lines. It would be quite proper for the accounts of the Trans-Canada Air Lines to be shown as part of the Canadian National Railways, as a wholly-owned subsidiary; and in fact I would think that in ordinary bookkeeping they should be.
The president of the Trans-Canada Air Lines is an official who gives his whole time to the Trans-Canada Air Lines. The controller of the Trans-Canada Air Lines, on the other hand, is a man who, according to his own estimate, gives one-twelfth of his time to the Trans-Canada Air Lines and the remainder of his time to the Canadian National Railways. A number of the officials hold corresponding positions in the two organizations. For that reason it seems both impractical and contrary to ordinary business procedure to have one minister in charge of the large organization which controls entirely, so far as the business end is concerned, the smaller organization, and to have another minister responsible for that smaller organization. Yet that is the situation. According to what the minister has now said, the Canadian National Railways comes under the Minister of Transport, and the Trans-Canada Air Lines, a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Canadian National Railways, comes under the Minister of Trade and Commerce. No matter what the arrangements have been, I suggest that it would be appropriate that a statement be made by the government that this situation will be rectified and that the Trans-Canada Air Lines will be brought under the same minister who is responsible for the administration of the Canadian National Railways.

Here when we deal with the estimates, the first item is always general administration. I am just asking hon. members to consider whether they would not prefer to have the item of general administration in each department deferred until the individual items had been dealt with. Then in the light of the information that would have been elicited with respect to each item, I think there could be a more satisfactory discussion of general administration.
I am not asking for a decision by hon. members at this time; but it has occurred to me that it might be helpful if, in committee, we went into the individual items and on those individual items obtained the information available. With that, I think we would be in a better position to discuss the general administration and it would also enable us probably to avoid some of the duplication. The detailed information would have been obtained on each of the headings, and everyone would then have had that information with which to enable him to form his own opinion about the general administration of the department. I think he would then be in a better position to make objective suggestions as to the way in which he might feel the general administration of the department could be improved.
As I say, I am not asking hon. members to agree to that procedure for the time being; but I believe that if they will just give it some thought, it might recommend itself to them. We on our part would be quite prepared to allow the item of general administration in each department to stand, and to have the general discussion after the individual items had been passed and after the information sought by hon. members had been given on those individual items.

May I point out to the Prime Minister, Mr. Chairman, that there is one serious objection to any such plan, and it is this. Ever since I have been here, the practice has been that most of the estimates go through in the last week or two of the

session, and there is absolutely no opportunity for a proper discussion on those estimates. Over the last year or two a system has been worked out whereby, on each department, there is a general review of the whole department on the administration item; one day has been set aside for each department. For example, today we have the Department of Transport estimates up just for that purpose, namely, a general review. When that review has taken place, ordinarily it does not take long to get through the individual items. If, on the other hand, we try to do the individual items first, I think the Prime Minister will find that there will be a long debate on every single individual item or on most of the individual items, and the result might be a great deal more delay than we have under the present system. Then when it came to a general review of the department at the end of the session, there would be no time in which to conduct such a review.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There may be objections, but I would ask hon. members just to consider the alternative of taking the individual items first, getting the information about them and then having a discussion on the general administration of the department after that information has been obtained. There are objections to any course. There are objections to there not being more time available to deal with the estimates. But there are so many matters that hon. members wish to have discussed at considerable length on the floor of the house that I am sure each of us endeavours to have the best use made of the time available.

May I just suggest this. There is certainly a great deal to be given consideration in regard to ways in which we can facilitate the handling of the various items. There are reasons why it is advisable to discuss certain things at the beginning, and I can see reasons for deferring certain aspects of the discussion. But just before we rise, might I earnestly suggest that some consideration be given to the situation which arises from having the Trans-Canada Air Lines under one minister and the Canadian National Railways under another; because among the accounts that we shall be examining in the Department of Transport are the accounts dealing with aeronautics and civil aviation generally. I suggest that, even at this stage, the desirability of bringing these two together might be given some consideration.

Mr. Chairman, on rising at this time I cannot content myself with the negative statement that I had not intended to do so. I want to assert affirmatively that I had not intended to speak in these protracted debates on these bills to incorporate the pipe line companies. My reason for changing that intention is that a couple of hours ago a newspaper story published in this morning's Gazette was brought to my attention. This newspaper story is at page 11 of today's issue, and bears the title, "Gardiner Said to Be Demanding All-Canadian Pipe Lines Route". It purports to be a report of the proceedings of a Liberal caucus held last Wednesday morning.
Now, all hon. members know that the deliberations of party caucuses are confidential, just as are the deliberations of council. I am quite sure that no one who attended that caucus ever informed anyone, outside of party members, of anything that transpired within the walls of the hall where it was held. So the whole story about what goes on in our caucus, just as any story about what goes on in the caucuses of any other of the parties, must be the writer's guesswork in that respect.
He would not expect me, I am sure, and no one else would expect me to say anything here about what went on in that caucus, either by way of confirmation or by way of denial. I think the security and the confidential character of caucuses is best preserved by abstaining from confirming or denying any of these newspaper stories, and just leaving them, as it is best to leave any other trial balloons or kites, to explode or break up in consequence of their own inherent weaknesses rather than do anything positive to hasten that result.
But this story contained more than a purported report of what took place in caucus. It has this paragraph:
The high degree of interest in these reports out of caucus stems from the fact that, up to the present, the government had made it plain that it felt that parliament should give the two companies a free hand in selecting the route along which they would build the huge pipe line. And both the

Prairie Transmission Lines Alberta Natural Gas Company and Prairie Transmission Lines, Limited, have made it equally plain that they would prefer to use a route through the United States to the Pacific coast, ostensibly because of higher costs involved for the Canadian route, but perhaps with an eye to tapping rich, inland United States markets.
I do not know what the companies have made plain. I did not attend the meetings of the committees. I have not seen any of the promoters of these companies. I have not read the testimony taken in committee, nor the report of the committee. I do know that if anyone in the press gallery had come to the conclusion that the government had made it plain that it felt that parliament should give the two companies a free hand to select the route along which they would build the huge pipe line others may have reached the same conclusion, and I feel I am called upon to point out that there was no such thing made plain by the government, nor ever intended to be made plain by the government.
The position of the government has been quite otherwise, and I am going to make a statement here, lest there might be others than members of the press gallery who might have assumed that there was anything of that character made plain in the attitude of the government.
The article goes on to say:
The Progressive Conservative, C.C.F. and Social Credit members, who have resorted to an outright filibuster to hold up the bills-and succeeded throughout last session-have offered many times to pass the bills without delay as soon as the government or sponsors of the bills gave assurances that the all-Canadian route would be used.
Well, I am not going to say anything about whether there has been a filibuster or not. There has been protracted discussion, we know, and it has gone over quite a long period of time. But, be that as it may, the sponsor of the bill cannot, of course, give an assurance where the pipe line will be built. The government can give no assurance whatsoever. To attempt to give such assurance would be practically contempt of parliament.
Parliament last year determined that this matter would be one to be turned over to the board of transport commissioners; and for the government to attempt to usurp the functions of the board of transport commissioners would be contempt of the will of parliament expressed in the Pipe Lines Act.
Now, so that there may be no doubt about that, let us see what we are faced with. These companies are to be incorporated, and to have certain corporate powers. The bills-this one and the other-are in practically the same terms; and those passed last year were in the same terms. This one states:
The company shall have all the powers, privileges and immunities conferred by, and be subject


to all the limitations, liabilities and provisions of any general legislation which is enacted by parliament, relating to pipe lines for the transmission and transportation of gas and oil or any liquid product or by-product thereof.
And then it says:
The company, subject to the provisions of any general legislation which is enacted by parliament, relating to pipe lines for the transmission and transportation of gas and oil or any liquid product or by-product thereof-
Shall have such-and-such powers. Now, parliament determined that any company which is incorporated would be subject to the various sections of the Pipe Lines Act, which is chapter 20 of the statutes of 1949. The act provides that "board" in the Pipe Lines Act means the board of transport commissioners. Section 11 of the Pipe Lines Act provides that:
A company shall not, except as in this act otherwise provided, begin the construction of a section or part of a company pipe line, until,
(a)	the board has by order granted the company leave to construct the line;
(b)	the plan, profile and book of reference of the section or part of the proposed line have been approved by the board; and
(c)	copies of the plan, profile and book of reference so approved, duly certified as such by the secretary of the board, have been deposited in the offices of the registrars of deeds for the districts or counties through which such section or part of the company pipe line is to pass.
Now, what has to be done when application is made for leave to build a pipe line, or any part of a pipe line? Section 12 of the Pipe Lines Act states:
(1)	Upon an application for an order granting leave to construct a line, the company shall file with the board a map showing the general location of the proposed line, the termini, and all cities, towns, villages, railways and navigable waters through, under or across which the line is to pass.
(2)	The company shall file a copy of the application and of the map with the attorney general of each province to which the application relates in whole or in part, and the board shall require notice of the application to be given by publication in newspapers or otherwise.
(3)	Upon the application, the board shall have regard to all considerations that appear to it to be relevant and in particular to the objection of any party interested, to a public interest that in the board's opinion may be affected by the granting or the refusing of the application, and to the financial responsibility of the applicant.
(4)	The decision of the board as to whether a person is or is not a party interested within the meaning of this section is binding and conclusive.
(5)	Where the board grants leave to construct a line, it may impose such terms and conditions as it considers proper and may limit the time within which the company shall construct and complete the line.
When that application has been granted, that and nothing else can be done. If there is to be any deviation whatsoever, then under section 20 the same procedure has to be followed to obtain leave to deviate from the line. However, this is subject to the right

of the board to give an exemption provided the deviation is merely intended to straighten out a curve or to lessen a grade. I quote partly from subsection 3 of that section as follows:
-if such deviation, change or alteration does not exceed 300 yards from the centre line of the company pipe line, located or constructed in accordance with the plans, profiles and books of reference approved by the board under this act.

Those are the provisions that apply to any company that gets a charter from this parliament. By that statute parliament placed jurisdiction and responsibility for considering the whole question upon the board of transport commissioners. I assume that, at the time it was considered by parliament, the board of transport commissioners would be a competent board to discharge that kind of responsibility. I think it should be realized by the people of Alberta and the people of British Columbia, who are naturally gravely concerned about the proper development and use of their natural resources, that parliament has put upon the board of transport commissioners the responsibility of examining applications and objections and all information necessary to arrive at a proper decision.
This is the same board to which the people of those provinces applied with success not so long ago to have remedied one of their traditional grievances, the mountain differential in freight rates. That matter had been referred to many times in this house, but that also was something in connection with which parliament had placed responsibility and jurisdiction in the board of transport commissioners. The people of Alberta and British Columbia rightly went to that board and made their case and I am informed that the decision gave them satisfaction in respect of that grievance. It is the same board.
If parliament feels at this or any time that that board is not competent to do the right kind of job, the way to remedy that situation is to amend the Pipe Lines Act and not to attempt by discriminating in favour
Prairie Transmission Lines of one or against another company to do it in a partial way. Three charters in practically the same terms as those in the bill before us were granted at the last session of parliament and each of those charters is subject to the legislation then existing or to such future legislation as parliament might choose to enact with respect to pipe lines. If there is to be another tribunal or another board that would determine these matters, then the taking of such a step should be settled by amending the Pipe Lines Act.
As to the very interesting question as to whether the topography of our country is such that it permits the building of a pipe line without going outside our territory, I am sure that not only the people of British Columbia and Alberta but the people of all Canada would rejoice in that kind of decision.
It is not only the people of Quebec and New Brunswick who have deplored the fact that the Canadian Pacific had to run through Maine to get to New Brunswick; that was something which concerned the people of the whole dominion. It was because of their feelings in that respect that the Canadian National took the long course through the valley of the Matapedia adding a great many miles to the distance. Nevertheless they provided an all-Canadian route. It was for that reason that the route traced for the transcontinental railway when it was built some forty years ago goes through the county of Temis-couata and into New Brunswick without departing at any time from Canadian soil. That is a thing which I think is of satisfaction to us all.
I am not going to suggest that the protracted debates in this parliament about the desirability of an all-Canadian pipe line for the gas and oil of Alberta has been a waste of time. It has aroused public opinion as to the desirability of doing that if it is possible. I would expect that that would not be lost from the point of view of the members of the board of transport commissioners and that they would not lightly disregard the unanimous desires of Canadians that their own territory be used to the greatest possible advantage. I would expect that when they got an application and before they approved anything, they would want to be shown that there is or there is not a practicable way of doing it without going out of Canada. I would expect that they will require the applicants to satisfy them that surveys of the various routes mentioned in this discussion have been made.
I do not claim to know enough about the topographical conditions, about the mountain passes, to be able to formulate an opinion as to whether or not they present insuperable
2230	HOUSE OF
Prairie Transmission Lines difficulties. But if I were a member of a board charged by parliament with the responsibility of making that kind of decision and were called upon to exercise my judgment, I would want pretty full evidence that it could not be done in Canada before I would put my signature to a plan or project that was not going to be carried out in Canada.
I suggest that unless and until we come to the conclusion that the board of transport commissioners cannot be entrusted with that kind of responsibility, because we do not feel that they are either competent enough to do it properly or sufficiently imbued with the spirit of the Canadian people to want to do it properly, the thing for us to do is to amend the Pipe Lines Act in a manner that will apply to every company that secures a charter for a pipe line and not in a manner that will discriminate in favour of one against another. Perhaps one has to say in words what one wants to have regarded as plain. I am speaking as one of the members of the government, and I want to make it plain that I have sufficient confidence in the board of transport commissioners to vote for the passage of these bills. I am not asking anyone to follow my example, but I am suggesting that my reason for doing so is not because I am determining where the pipe lines are going to be built but because I feel that the board which parliament selected only a year ago to discharge that responsibility is competent to do so, and will discharge it in a manner that will do justice to all Canadian citizens.
