The hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra asked me earlier this afternoon for a statement on the results of shipping and shipbuilding policy. At short notice it is of course impossible for me to make a comprehensive statement at this time, but I can give him a few facts.
Canadian shipping policy was stated to this house by the Prime Minister on December 9 last. It is not necessary for me to give the reasons for such policy, as they were very fully stated at the time.
We cannot hear.

In passing, however, I might remind the house that the Canadian costs of operation are about double British costs, and in order to maintain the Canadian shipping industry it was decided to permit owners to transfer to United Kingdom flag, and to subsidize not more than forty Canadian flag ocean-going vessels at a cost of not more than $3 million.
At the time of such statement there were 174 Canadian owned ocean-going vessels. Two were sold since that date and the proceeds deposited in escrow pursuant to the replacement plan, leaving 172 ships. Transfers to United Kingdom flag have been approved in respect of 93 ships, and transfers in respect of 23 ships are still pending.
Payment of subsidies are of course subject to vote of parliament, and the sum of $3 million has been included in the current estimates of the Canadian maritime commission for that purpose. Subject to such vote the Canadian maritime commission has approved subsidies in respect of 31 vessels and nine subsidy applications are still pending. Applications for subsidy in respect of 16 vessels have been declined on the ground that the applicant vessels do not employ Canadian crews.
[Mr. Cruickshank.l
Can the minister file a list of the vessels for which subsidy has been granted?

Yes, I can eventually, but I cannot do it immediately. It will take some time to get the list, because they are in course of being dealt with from day to day.
Prior to the coming into effect of the shipping policy there were forty Canadian vessels laid up for lack of employment. Today there are only twelve laid up, and I have no doubt that these will move shortly when employment offers.
I do not propose to comment upon the results of the shipping policy except to say that to my knowledge a number of Canadian shipowners have expressed themselves as being more than satisfied with such policy as being the only reasonable method whereby the shipping industry may be kept alive in Canada.
In so far as the shipbuilding and ship repair industries are concerned, there are at the moment about 9,000 men employed in Canadian yards. In its annual report last year the Canadian maritime commission stated that it would be necessary to maintain employment at a level of not less than 7,000 men in order to preserve the industry.
It is difficult for me to state what effect the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act has had upon shipbuilding generally. It is impossible for anyone to say that any particular ship owner has commenced building because of the provisions of that act. I think it may be sufficient for me to state that at the present time shipbuilding orders totalling more than $67 million are in preparation or under construction in Canadian shipyards.

Mr. Chairman, after the discussion of the last hour I wish to devote a short time to a matter which, I am sure, will be regarded as non-controversial, and it probably will receive the same support it received some three or four months ago when I spoke on this subject. I refer to the establishment of a Canadian coastguard.
I am certain this subject is of interest not only to my part of the country but, indeed, to every section of Canada; and I say that because the few words I delivered at the last session on the subject were of such a character that everyone in the house read them- they must have, because I heard so many comments from people who did not read them.
I hope hon. members will excuse my early return to this subject because of what is happening in connection with the coastguard. It is very difficult for hon. members to realize, in view of the size of Canada, the extent of our coast line. Canada is the third largest

country in the world, and it has the greatest coast line of any country. By "coast line" I mean of course not only the sea coast, but the coast lines of the great lakes. Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and British Columbia are bordered by the sea.
Manitoba.

Manitoba? Probably so. Then, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland are islands in the Atlantic. Ontario is bounded by the great lakes in the south and by Hudson bay and James bay in the north. It has a very extensive coast line. In fact, to my knowledge-not from personal knowledge, but from reading-the only provinces which have no coast line are Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Very obviously therefore there is necessity for a coastguard for a country like Canada. If this pipe line is built other than in Canada I would not be surprised if we were to need a pipe line guard for the pipe line. As all hon. members will recollect, there is over the doorway of the parliament buildings the inscription, "From Sea to Sea". In other words, Canada is a great maritime nation and, in keeping with the traditions of maritime nations, it should have a coastguard.
The understanding I gained at the last session from statements made by the Minister of Transport was that a coastguard service would be entirely too expensive and out of line with the duty it would perform. It must be obvious that such a statement is ridiculous. I say that in all honesty and without knowing the extent to which the minister has gone into the matter.
One thing we must remember is that a coastguard is a service for the saving of life; and when the saving of life and the saving of dollars are matters under consideration, there should be no alternative. I think all hon. members will agree with that, particularly when we see the tremendous expenditures being made every day for services not nearly as important as the coastguard.
As all hon. members know, the present coastguard service is being carried on by the marine section of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. As I said some months ago- and I say it honestly, as I am sure all hon. members will-there can be no question as to the reliability and the wonderful record of that great force. We have to remember, however, that this is a question of a sea force, and is not and should not be part of the job of the police force.
All hon. members are aware of the United States coastguard. In peacetime it operates under the treasury, and in wartime under the navy. As an adjunct to the navy it is of

course very important, and plays a great part in time of war. I do not need to go into the question of what they did' in the last war. Hon. members will recall the stories of submarine landings, or attempted landings in the United States, and the handling of them by the coastguard.
The suggestion of a Canadian coastguard has been mooted for many years. Back in the days of the Bovey commission they recommended that a committee be set up by the government to consider that matter. Since that time organizations throughout the country have requested the establishment of such a service.
The last time this matter was before the house was March 22, 1950, when, as reported at page 999, the hon. member for Queens-Shelburne directed this question to the minister:
1.	Have any steps been taken towards setting up a joint committee representing the departments of fisheries, transport, and national defence, for the purpose of unifying and improving the coastal protection service?
2.	If so, has such a committee been set up?
3.	Has the committee been instructed to investigate improvements in the protective service for fishermen?
4.	If so, will consideration be given to the provision of a radio-equipped and all-weather sea rescue and emergency towing service for small fishing craft?
5.	When will the recommendations of this committee be made known, and when will action be taken to implement such recommendations?
The answer given by the minister was that such a committee had been set up. I understand it has been established for over a year now.
An interdepartmental committee has been set up to review the present arrangements for search and rescue and to make recommendations for improved and more efficient service.
The search and rescue is intended to cover all seafarers operating off the Canadian coasts.
The terms of reference of this committee quoted in part 2 above are sufficiently embracing to cover this consideration.
The recommendations of this committee will shortly be available when the action required to implement them will be considered.
That was a fair question to which a fair answer was made, but I wonder how long "shortly" is in the minds of the government. The committee has been at work now for almost a year and on March 22 it was stated the report was to be released shortly. If the minister cares to reply I hope he will tell us how long "shortly" is in the minds of the government.
On behalf of the newest province I ask the minister to consider, apart altogether from whatever the recommendations of the committee may be, the setting up of a coastguard service based somewhat on the United States

coastguard service. Newfoundland has a coast line 6,000 miles long which is very rough in places and subject to nasty weather at times. There are sections in which there are very few harbours, and that creates dangerous conditions. The fleet which goes to the Grand Banks now faces serious competition from European trawlers who have increased tremendously and are encroaching on the grounds of our fishermen. There have been a number of incidents such as the cutting of a man's trawl and others which go to the extent of endangering the safety of our own fishermen.
Labrador is becoming of paramount importance to the economy of Canada mainly because of the iron ore deposits in the interior and the Goose airport. It also has a difficult coast line and this matter should receive serious consideration. This matter has been discussed on many occasions, but I think it has come home to us more forcibly in recent years. I conclude by reading from a resolution of the dominion council of naval officers of Canada passed last summer at Halifax which reads:
It is not in accord with national dignity to be repeatedly obligated to the United States coastguard.
Those are my sentiments in this matter. It is time that Canada realized it was a maritime nation and we should lean less on Uncle Sam in connection with matters maritime.

had to receive the attention of the government. I am just as regretful at the fact that the committee has not been able to report as are those hon. members who are particularly interested in the subject of air rescue operations.

I do not wish to initiate a debate on this subject because I have spoken before. However, I should like to repeat what I said, that I believe we should proceed step by step to co-ordinate the various agencies we have at the present time which are working in this direction. I should like to stress that there is a degree of urgency at the present time because it has been announced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that a treaty with Japan may be signed in the not too distant future. There will then be the possibility of Japanese fishing fleets coming to our west coast waters and there will be need for greater protection of our own British Columbia fishermen. I shall not say any more than that.
Can the minister give us some idea as to how far the recommendations of the Kellock commission are going to be implemented? About two weeks ago he said that we would soon have an opportunity to know how the new regulations would fit into the recommendations made by that commission appointed to investigate the Noronic disaster. Various statements have been published in the press on the west coast which would indicate that rather strict regulations are going to be applied. These will have a distinct bearing on those people who live on islands. As a matter of fact a great many of my constituents live

on islands. Many of them are entirely dependent upon steamship service to move from one place to another and to receive all their supplies. Many of the steamships in this service have been in commission for a great many years. They are old vessels and if they have to add heavy new appliances it may be it will force some of them out of commission. They will be taken off the service with disastrous results to the people who are living on small islands in the strait of Georgia and also on Vancouver island.
I should like to point out that not only do Canadian vessels serve these people but also vessels under the United States flag which carry passengers and freight between these islands and the mainland. If our Canadian vessels were forced out of service by too stringent regulations then there would be an increase in the United States trade to the detriment of the Canadian service. I should like to have some explanation as to how far these regulations are going to be carried. I believe there is an escape clause. I do not know whether it will be helpful, but I have one suggestion to make. One of the greatest causes of fire at sea is the innumerable coats of paint which are put on vessels. Coat after coat of paint is placed on the sides and in the holds. I suggest there should be a regulation that there should never be more than four coats of paint on a vessel, and if there are any more they should be required to scrape them right off. Possibly the suggestion should be worthy of consideration because I know that an excessive number of coats of paint is one of the main causes of fire at sea.

I do not think the hon. member for Nanaimo need fear too greatly that ships will be taken out of operation because of the regulations. I am not saying that such will not be the case but I know of no such case at the moment. Some weeks ago I made a statement in the house shortly after the new regulations had been gazetted. I do not think the hon. member would want me to repeat it because he saw it. Generally speaking, perhaps I might say that it is the intention by the enactment of the steamship regulations appearing in the Canada Gazette to implement the recommendations of the Kel-lock commission so far as it is reasonably possible to do so.
In order to do that it was thought that if the safety of life at sea convention, which was approved by many nations at London and which I hope will be introduced this session as amendments to the Canada Shipping Act, could be implemented in regulations, we would be going a long distance in carrying out the recommendations of the Kellock report. We have tried to do that in the regulations that have been enacted. Of
Supply-Transport
course they are far more stringent and far more difficult of application that those in effect before the disastrous Noronic fire, so much so. that there has been some objection on the part of operators. However, after they made their representations to Ottawa I believe they came to the conclusion that the regulations we were making were not on the whole unfair. Certainly they came to the conclusion that they would do everything they could to abide by them, and I already have the assurance that that is being done by a large number of corporations.
There are cases-and I presume it is one of these my hon. friend has in mind-where ships are providing a service of convenience to the public, and if they had to follow all the regulations it might well be they would be put out of commission entirely. I think that the steamship inspectors will use some judgment in that regard because it is not the intention to discontinue any service which is required for the public unless, of course, there is a refusal on the part of the owner to comply with those of the regulations which appear to our inspectors to be fair and reasonable.
I want to say one word about the escape clause to which the hon. member referred. The escape clause was naturally put in there because we realize that it is impossible to meet all these regulations for the coming season. Some companies can meet some of them; others can meet all of them. I know of one company that has met practically all of them except one or two that it could not implement before the opening of navigation, but there are other ships that have few or none of these appliances. The object of the escape clause was to give the steamship inspection board some discretion in the application of the regulations. I repeat that at the moment I know of no steamship service that has been put out of operation because of the regulations. I would not want the committee to feel, however, that it is not the intention to put them into force. It is very much the intention to implement them, and if not fully this season at least by the time ships are put into commission next year.
There will be a reasonable length of time allowed? I am concerned primarily with small companies servicing the smaller islands in the strait of Georgia. There will be a reasonable length of time?
Yes, surely.

I would hope that we would not press the minister too hard not to enforce these regulations. If a disaster occurred in connection with the type of boat that plies between these islands and other points on the west coast it would not be of the same

Supply-Transport
magnitude as the Noronic tragedy. Nevertheless it would be a disaster and the first thing that would be asked would be whether the regulations were in force. The minister would be justly subject to criticism if, after the tragic warning we have had, he allowed ships that carry passengers to continue in service without complying with the necessary safety regulations.
I agree with the hon. member for Nanaimo that a certain amount of time should be allowed; but the companies or individuals operating these ships should at least indicate by this time that they are taking steps to comply with the regulations. If the minister finds any attempt to evade those regulations he will be derelict in his duty unless he sees that they are complied with. There is no use having regulations and then permitting marine inspectors or others whose duty it is to enforce them to neglect that duty. If it is necessary to provide a service to any of those islands, and that service cannot be provided without endangering the lives of passengers and crew, then this government should provide the service and safeguard the lives of the people who want to travel to those islands.
I should hope that we would not on the one hand criticize the ministers for such disasters as happened last year in Toronto, and then say now that there is danger you may put some boats out of business if you enforce regulations considered necessary for the safety of those who use those boats. I want to be absolutely fair with the minister. As long as the regulations are not beyond what is required, I hope he will see to it that they are enforced.

There is one point in regard to the regulations governing shipping that I think it would be appropriate to mention here, in view of the fact that subsequently we will be considering this matter in more detail. As I understand, the regulations that have been drafted require the provision of certain water facilities at points where passenger ships of a certain size and type will be docking, so that in event of a fire water will be available for the fire hoses. The point I should like to place before the minister for consideration is that it is necessary to do something more than merely assure adequate supplies of water for fire hoses when ships are in port. In certain famous cases ships have capsized at the dock because water was poured into them without some measure of control and supervision by those who understood the particular job of putting out fires in ships. I understand, for instance, that in the case of the Normandie, which caught fire when in dock in New York, actually it was the excessive load of water

that capsized it rather than anything directly connected with the fire itself. I believe the same thing happened in a very disastrous fire that occurred in a passenger ship at Chicago, and there have been a number of other cases.
It does not require very much imagination to see what might happen if enormous quantities of water were poured into a ship without an understanding of the difficulties that might arise. I am raising this question because it has been brought to my attention; and I merely place it before the minister at this time so that if it does call for consideration he will have an opportunity of going into it in some detail before we deal with the act itself.

I thank the leader of the opposition for his suggestion. I do not know whether he has had an opportunity of looking at the regulations, but they are divided into a series of clauses which provide first and foremost for fire-resisting bulkheads. That is really the thing that protects the ship more than anything else. They also provide for the installation of a sprinkler system. If all ships had been provided with steel, fire-resisting bulkheads, plus sprinkler systems, I think we would have gone a long way in avoiding those tragedies that have occurred. The regulations also provide for public address systems, automatic fire alarm systems, patrol musters and so on.
While I am on my feet I want to say I am grateful to the hon. member for Vancouver East for the attitude he has adopted. One must not forget that these regulations are difficult to apply. It is one thing to make regulations; it is another thing to apply them. It is when you start to apply them that you have all sorts of people say, "Oh, don't touch me; you'll put me out of business," or, "Don't touch me; these people on the east coast or the west coast won't have the service." For that reason I welcome the views of the hon. gentleman, because they recognize the difficulties of trying to administer such regulations.
That applies, of course, to existing ships, not to ships that may be built in the future. New ships certainly will comply with the regulations, and most new ships are built in such a way that it is not necessary to even think of applying them. The difficulty arises in connection with the ships already in existence, which in the past have been exempt from all new regulations. Now we are trying to apply new regulations to those ships, and that is where the difficulty of application comes in.

I know I would be misunderstood by the minister if I did not have something to say in reference to transportation.

However, dealing with the last matter that was discussed, that is the regulations concerning safety devices for boats, I might just point out that if these regulations were put into effect within the next ten days we would have no water communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. The only way we would be able to get across would be by air. So when these regulations are put into effect these boats, two of which belong to the government while the others belong to private concerns, will have to be given sufficient time to comply with them.
If I had been the first speaker on this item I would have offered a suggestion to the minister, and I think I will offer it even now. It is this. When a minister has his deputies and assistants sitting before him on the floor of the house, I believe the first thing he should do is introduce those gentlemen to the committee, so that we would know who they are. All they would have to do would be to take their bow after being introduced. I think the hon. minister should do that, so that we will know the gentlemen who are before us.
As I said a moment ago, transportation is one of the problems in which the province of Prince Edward Island is most interested. We are therefore interested in all the transport items under the minister. I see that for the year 1951 the estimates are higher by $6 million than for last year. No doubt this can be blamed on the tenth province, Newfoundland. However, that province has the right to a fair share, and this increase is allowable if the $6 million is going to be spent to improve transportation conditions in the new province of Newfoundland.
I notice that there is still that old blank cheque in the departmental estimates this year, amounting to $10,116,752, for temporary assistance. I have brought it to the attention of the house for the last four or five years, and I am pleased to note that this year the department lists the number of permanent positions in each department, as well as the number of temporaries. In the past we were never given any idea of the number of temporary assistants. In that connection an unfortunate thing arises in the estimates, in that another new class has been put in termed "casuals". I never noticed it before. I did not know the meaning of the word "casuals" so I looked up the dictionary and found that one of the meanings is "happy-go-luckies". It seems to me that is a suitable term for this item of "casuals", covering a period after an election year. Surely some breakdown should be given of that item because it is considerable. It amounts to $2,445,227 for this new form of
Supply-Transport
employees called "happy-go-luckies". We are called upon to give another blank cheque for over two and a half per cent of the total vote. I know the minister will explain that when he replies.
On April 20 a question was asked by the member for Prince about the dual ferry system, or as it is called the shuttle service, during the tourist season. I was astonished at the reply given by the minister. After granting the request for this shuttle system for a couple of months, he stated:
-I am instructing the Canadian National Railways to maintain records to establish the net financial results of the operation of the second ferry this year, and if the operating costs are not offset by additional revenues it is distinctly understood that the double service will not be authorized in 1951.
The minister has no right to make a statement of that kind. If he were to read the terms of confederation under which Prince Edward Island went into this union in 1873, he would find that the government is bound to give us that service. Neither he nor any other minister can say that if the service does not pay it will not be continued. The same thing could be said about the car ferry, yet the government of the dominion and the government of Prince Edward Island in 1873 pledged themselves to give that transportation service. As I have said many times on the floor of this house, there never has been a full implementation of those terms of confederation. The only attempt at implementation was the establishment of the car ferry operating between Borden and Tormentine by the government of R. L. Borden. When I hear the minister making statements of this type, that a second car ferry will not be operated in 1951 if it does not prove to be a paying proposition, I can tell him right now that if he tries to live up to that statement he will be subjected to a barrage that will make him think a second time before he makes such a statement.
I want to say this, and it has been said many times before, that men are on record with regard to our transportation question. I have an article here in which the Hon. Charles A. Dunning, while he was minister of railways and also representative of Queens county, made a statement at a public meeting in Charlottetown. He said this:
The only proper and satisfactory solution to give this island the service it is entitled to according to the terms of confederation of 1873 is an auxiliary service.
That means two boats. Remember this service cannot appear against us as a deficit as it now does, but I shall deal with that later. This article continues:
It is the essence of the Canadian partnership that the ferry rates as well as the service to and from the

Supply-Transport
province should be such as to relieve it, in so far as possible, of the disadvantages of its island position. Anything short of this makes for insularity.
The minister said, in his reply to the member for Prince, that he is instructing the Canadian National Railways. Instructions should be given to the Canadian National Railways, who are the subcontractors in this case just as they are the subcontractors in operating the Abegweit, that they are to give us the service not to yield a profit but to fulfil the terms of union. That service can be nothing less than a daily service, satisfactory to the province, and it should be supplied at the lowest possible cost, not to exceed the cost of operating this ferry as a bridge.
In addition to that, according to the terms of confederation, we are entitled to free transportation for all our products. We have not fought for it, but we will never be satisfied, nor will the province of Prince Edward Island have the terms of confederation fulfilled, until there is a government in power that will live up to those obligations. Year after year when these estimates are being passed, one finds a reference to a deficit in the operation of the ferry system.
I have spoken about this time and time again on previous occasions. It is not a deficit. It may be a deficit to government operation, but let us contrast it with the canals in Ontario and in Quebec. How much money is spent annually on canals? This year I think for the operating of the canals there is provided the sum of $8 million. How much profit do those canals bring in to the government? I understand there is no charge whatsoever for freight moving on those canals. I am not urging that there should be. But it is a service that the government of the Dominion of Canada promised and they are carrying it out in this respect.
Yet when it comes to the province of Prince Edward Island, what do they do? As to the car ferry, we never see a statement showing whether it is a loss or a profit. We are obliged to take the word of the subcontractors. That deficit stands out like a sore thumb. It should be put in there, just the same as is done with reference to canals; it should go in there as a ferry service and not as a deficit; it looks to the rest of the provinces as if Prince Edward Island was getting a hand-out year by year on this deficit.
I am not going to labour this point much further. I still hope that some of these men in the offices, if the minister refuses to take it up himself, will see that it is a service and that the deficit can be charged back to the

consolidated revenue fund, as it should be, the same as the deficit on the canals and canal systems.
I might also mention that we have every proof to show that our province has been discriminated against by all the different provinces. As we come along to the different items, I am going to deal with some of those then. At the present time I just wish to bring this matter to the attention of the minister, and I hope he will give my request some favourable consideration. I hope he will be able to see the difference between a deficit and a service.

Before this general item is carried, I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport one item which comes under his jurisdiction, namely the matter of the extension of certain C.N.R. lines in northeastern Saskatchewan. The lines that I particularly refer to are the C.N.R. lines from Saskatoon through Melfort to Carrot River and the C.N.R. line from Canora through Sturgis to Arborfield. Those two lines were built back in the period after the first war, between 1923 and 1926. At that time it was expected that the lines would be extended through to The Pas in Manitoba to connect up with the Hudson Bay railway at that point. It is some twenty-five to twenty-seven years since those lines were built. Today they still end at the same point as when they were first built; that is at Carrot River and Arborfield.
Today the settlement has extended out from those two points for some thirty or forty miles, and today they are two of the heaviest delivery points for grain in the province of Saskatchewan. Last year at both of these points approximately one and a quarter million bushels of wheat were delivered. As the minister will see, a great deal of this grain must be delivered from long distances. As a matter of fact the settlement now extends for some thirty or forty miles in a fanshape northeasterly from those two points and the settlement now has spread out so that it extends to about the economical distance from which grain can be hauled to any delivery point. The settlement will stop where it now is until these two lines are extended.
There are two good reasons why these lines should be extended at this time. Northeast of Carrot River there has been a large settlement of returned men established on co-operative farms. There are some seven to ten of these co-operative farms, with ten to twelve settlers and their families on each farm. Some
30,000	acres are being brought under cultivation there. These men in delivering their grain

have to haul it a distance of from twenty-five to thirty-five miles to their nearest delivery point.
There is also in the province of Saskatchewan a tremendous demand for new land to which could be moved settlers from the dried-out areas who have for a great many years been receiving assistance under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. This is one of the only areas left in Saskatchewan of good land to which these settlers can be moved.
I have here a report of a speech made by Mr. L. B. Thomson, P.F.R.A. director. This speech was made at the 45th annual convention of the Saskatchewan association of rural municipalities. In it, in speaking of this development in the northeastern part of Carrot River, he stated:
"This development I regard as one of the most important; it will add greatly to the resettlement needs of Saskatchewan," Mr. Thomson said. The reclamation could be undertaken at a low cost per acre, according to the surveys now completed, he stated.
Mr. Thomson reviewed rehabilitation activities in Saskatchewan since 1935, and particularly since establishment of P.F.R.A. in 1938. There were still "hundreds of farmers" requiring resettlement and rehabilitation assistance, for all that had been done, he stressed.
Mr. Thomson has stated that in this area there are approximately one million acres of new land that can be brought under cultivation; but this land will not be brought under cultivation unless these railway lines are extended to the point where transportation will be available to new settlers.
I would urge the minister to take this matter up with the Canadian National Railways officials, if it is they who are responsible for the extension of these lines, and have something done in the near future. Here we have some of the most valuable land in western Canada lying idle simply because of lack of transportation which could be provided by the spending of a few million dollars for the extension of these lines through to The Pas in Manitoba, which would make it possible for this land to be brought under cultivation.
It would save the government money, through being able to re-establish in that area hundreds of families from the dried-out area in the southern part of the province to whom at present they are having to pay P.F.A.A. assistance practically every year. It is estimated by the prairie farm rehabilitation people that there are in the southeastern part of Saskatchewan approximately 4,000 families who need to be re-established. Here we have the land'available. It is good land, land on which there has never been a crop failure; it is some of the most productive
Supply-Transport
land there is anywhere in western Canada. As a matter of fact, over the past twenty-five years the average crop yield in this area has been, in many cases, thirty bushels to the acre of wheat. It seems a waste to see this land lying idle simply because of the failure of the Canadian National Railways to extend these branch lines through to their logical point at The Pas in Manitoba. I would urge the minister to give consideration to this matter.

I am glad to have the hon. member's representations with reference to these two branch lines. I have not had an opportunity of discussing fully the branch lines program of the Canadian National Railways this year. I am afraid however that it will not be any more extensive than it was last year. When I make that statement I have in mind a statement made by the president of the Canadian National Railways before the committee on railways and shipping-or perhaps it was before the royal commission on transportation, I am not sure. In any event I shall be glad to bring these lines to the attention of the Canadian National Railways.
Who is responsible for the extension of those lines? Does the government make the decision, or do "the Canadian National Railways themselves make the decision?

The Canadian National
Railways must first of all submit the extension to the government. The reasons for submitting the extensions I have placed on Hansard on more than one occasion. First they must have some guarantee that there will be favourable returns from the operation. Next there must be some assurance that because of the density of the area to be served, natural resources and the like, there is the possibility of profitable operation and, finally, if it is a railway which is exclusively built for the development of natural resources, and one which is not their concern at all, they will so indicate to us and we will have to decide for ourselves whether it should be built or not. But in all of these lines-and I am referring of course to lines of the Canadian National Railways-it has been the practice to get the opinion of the railways as to whether they should be advanced.

Has anything been done
to relieve the Canadian National Railways from operating the Portland, Maine, division, and the terminal at Portland, Maine? This division and the terminal have lost money every year, and I understand they are
2244

Supply-Transport
still losing money. The railways own valuable property on the waterfront at Portland. They have eight or ten long freight sheds, which are not kept in repair. Why would it not be a good idea to get rid of this Portland, Maine, terminal? It is taking business away from Saint John and Halifax, and is being maintained at a loss to the taxpayers of Canada.

I am afraid if I were to go into the reasons in answer to the question the hon. member has brought up, we would get far afield. As the hon. member knows, there is a committee which deals with the affairs of the Canadian National Railways. Officers are brought before that committee for the very purpose of giving this information. I have not those officers before me, and neither have I that information. However, it was available before the committee. I do not know whether the hon. member asked for it, but it seems to me there was some discussion at that time on the Portland, Maine, interests of the Canadian National Railways. I hope my hon. friend will not insist upon an answer, because we could go on indefinitely in a discussion of that matter.

I asked the question in committee. Mr. Dingle said that we have had some offers for these sheds. I believe to date nothing concrete has developed. Mr. Donald Gordon said he would take my suggestion under advisement. However, this has been going on for years. They have been losing all kinds of money in the operation of that terminal. Why should the taxpayers of Canada pay for this loss, when it is only taking away freight which could go to the maritime ports of Saint John and Halifax?

I should like to say a few words regarding branch lines, because I believe I have more unfinished branch lines in my constituency than there are probably in any other constituency. It is easy to understand why that is so. It is due to the fact that this has been a drought area, and a great portion of the population have moved out.
For instance, there was the line built from Eyre to Acadia Valley. A train has run over that line once a week. The grade went on in a southwesterly direction from Acadia Valley, and I think it was headed toward Buffalo, but apparently it got lost on the way, because it ends in the middle of the prairie, and has never been completed.
Another line was built from Coronation to Youngstown. That line was completed, but no train has ever run over it. Now it is quite a job to find the track; it is all grown over.
Then, a line was built from Unity to Bodo, and a train has run over that once a week. The survey was carried on from there to Bulwark through Airways, and there is a lot of interest in that line. The farmers were anxious that it should be built. Some work was done, but nothing more has been done for many years. We are hoping that that line will be completed, because there is a considerable quantity of stock in that area, and when the Red Deer diversion scheme is carried out the whole economic picture will change.
I suppose we will have to wait for any more work being done on that line until the Red Deer diversion program is gone ahead with. The line I wish to speak about particularly is that from Loverna to Scapa. That line was built in the twenties, and for one year trains ran right through. But there was a stretch of twenty-four miles from Spondin to Hem-aruka, which was never ballasted. After the first year no more trains were run right through. The trains ran from Unity to Hemaruka, and then turned into Saskatchewan. The train continued to run from Scapa to Spondin, taking wheat out from the elevators. No trains have since then been run from Spondin to Hemaruka.
There has been a good deal of agitation to have that piece of line completed by way of ballasting. I have had communications in the past with Mr. Vaughan, and he stated it would cost about $600,000 to complete it. He said, however, there was not enough business to justify that expenditure, owing to the fact that the line was paralleled by the C.P.R. about eighteen miles to the north, and by the C.N.R. line to the south. He admitted at that time that if the Red Deer diversion scheme were put through there might be sufficient change in the economic picture to justify completing that line. That was the picture two or three years ago.
This spring, however, the C.N.R. made application to the board of transport commissioners to abandon the line from Spondin to Hemaruka, and I understand that permission was granted. The thing the farmers in that area are concerned about is this: What will be the freight rates from the towns east of Hemaruka on freight going west? In the past the practice has been that, in view of the fact that the C.N.R. did not run the trains west, and in view of the fact that the farmers at Hemaruka and east wanted to ship their stock to Calgary and to ship in coal from Drumheller, they were given the same freight rate as though the trains had actually run west to Scapa.

The C.N.R. only charged a freight rate on coal shipped in from Drumheller via Saskatchewan as if it had gone direct through Scapa. The same rate is charged on stock shipped to Calgary. Now there is the fear that, in view of the fact that the railway between Spondin and Hemaruka is to be abandoned, that preferred rate will no longer be allowed. Many petitions have been sent in asking that the preferential rate be adopted in the future. I took this matter up with the minister a few weeks ago and he said he would take it up with the railroad. Can he give the committee any information as to what will be the policy in regard to freight going west on this line?

I should like to support the plea made by the hon. member for Acadia as the people in the south of my constituency are interested in this same line and I have had many representations from them. Just across the river at the north of my constituency there are two other lines that have been referred to by many hon. members during the past number of years; I refer to the Hindville and Bonnyville route. Perhaps the minister can tell us something about that.

I am afraid I cannot make any more of a reply to the hon. member who has just taken his seat than I could to the hon. member for Melfort. When we were discussing the motion of the hon. member for Gaspe a few days ago I stated the reasons given by the Canadian National Railways for extensions or new construction. This will be found on page 1697 of Hansard. I have not had an opportunity of discussing fully with the president of the Canadian National Railways the branch lines program of the railroad for 1950, but I am afraid it will not be any more extensive than it was last year.
The hon. member for Acadia took up with me the question of freight rates arising out of the abandonment of the line he has mentioned. I have received no report as yet from the officials of the Canadian National Railways. When I do, I shall be glad to convey it to him.

This afternoon I made brief mention of a point which I think should be referred to in some detail before we pass on to the general items. This subject matter is embraced by later items in the estimates without being covered fully by any particular item. I refer to the fact that while the Canadian National Railways is under the Department of Transport, the Trans-Canada Air Lines, which is a fully-owned subsidiary of the Canadian National Railways, is under the Department of Trade and Commerce.
I submit that it is not just a question of which minister is going to be charged with 55946-1432
Supply-Transport
such ministerial responsibility as is necessary in connection with either of these activities. I suggest that there are obvious and strong reasons why it is of the utmost importance that these activities now under the Department of Trade and Commerce-the Trans-Canada Air Lines-should also be brought under the Department of Transport.
Within a day or two we shall have before us for consideration amendments to the Aeronautics Act. I do not propose to discuss them now, but without bending the rules too severely I think I can say that they are intended to extend the activities, both of the board and of the minister who will be responsible for the administration of the act. Having said that, I can then explain what I have in mind by reference to the act as it now stands.
The substantial amendments to the Aeronautics Act which were introduced in 1944 were the subject of heated controversy. Those amendments made the air transport board much more than a semi-judicial board dealing with problems presented to it in connection with the granting of licences and so on. The amendments of 1944 to the Aeronautics Act made the air transport board an agency of the minister who would be charged with administering that act.
Many of the most important functions of the board are stated to be subject to the approval of the minister. Regulations and various things of that kind are all brought under ministerial or governmental supervision. Moreover, the board conducts investigations and surveys for the purpose of determining where routes will go and where developments will take place, and that again is subject to the direction of the minister. All this means that the minister charged with the administration of the Aeronautics Act is also charged with responsibility for investigations which will result in the development of new routes, the extension of air services and things of that kind. Without going into the details of the proposed amendments, they will widen rather than diminish that administrative responsibility.
I submit that when government policy, right or wrong, has been to have a chosen instrument operate the main air routes of Canada, it is wholly unsound to have that chosen instrument under one minister and have the administration of the Aeronautics Act and investigations and surveys and inquiries relating to the extension of services called for by that act in the hands of another minister.
Let us take what is perhaps the least important aspect of the problem which is raised by this unnecessary divorcing of

Supply-Transport
similar activities. It means that on the one hand you have of necessity experts in the department charged with the responsibility for Trans-Canada Air Lines dealing with their affairs-now the Department of Trade and Commerce-and you have on the other hand of necessity experts in aviation and in the practical problems of aviation carrying out duties assigned to the Department of Transport under the Aeronautics Act. That in itself is a wasteful separation of services which could much more effectively and much more economically be brought together.
Then again you have the situation where the extension of branch lines of the Trans-Canada Air Lines is determined at the present time by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, with whatever approval is required from the government. On the other hand, under the Aeronautics Act the Minister of Transport is charged with the responsibility for conducting surveys, inquiries and other investigations which might lead to the extension of routes. Again, Mr. Chairman, without going into the details of the amending act, the responsibility of the Minister of Transport under the Aeronautics Act is now and will still more be, assuming that the amending act comes into effect, to reach out beyond the boundaries of Canada and seek arrangements under which air routes may be established for the chosen instrument and presumably for other air services as well. It seems to me this is unbusinesslike, wasteful of money and separates groups of experts who obviously should be brought together within one department so that their combined skill may be serving the one purpose of advancing aviation in Canada in every way possible.
Having said that, I am bringing this up in the discussion of the opening item of the estimates of the department because I still most earnestly ask the government to give consideration to the suggestion that the Minister of Transport should be the minister designated to supervise the activities of Trans-Canada Air Lines. I urge that this decision should be made before we reach the point in the estimates where we are discussing details of civil aviation and the Aeronautics Act, and that we should also have the decision made before we are called upon to discuss the amendments to the Aeronautics Act which will have a very great bearing on this subject. If we as Canadians had every reason to be satisfied with our position in the field of civil aviation today it might well be said that no convincing argument was put forward why we should be looking for any change in administrative arrangements or other details of that kind. But, Mr. Chairman, in the interests of the future of aviation in this

country and the future of our air services extended beyond our own bounds, I think we should approach the problem with the knowledge that we have not succeeded as we should have in extending Canadian air services throughout the world in the years since the war.
I think it is time for us to face the situation frankly. We ended the war with the greatest pool of trained pilots, aircrew and ground personnel per capita of any nation in the world. I think history clearly demonstrates that there is something about the very type of country in which we live, the very kind of people that we are, which gives to Canadians some special skill in this great new field of transportation. In the infancy of aviation in the first world war Canadian pilots, some of whom are sitting in this house as members of parliament, demonstrated qualities not only equal but superior to any found in active service in that war. It was from among the young veterans of that war that our great bush air service developed which was an inspiration to the whole world in what could be dene by the energy and vision of courageous young men.
Canada reached great heights in aviation in the years before the second world war. Today .Canadians sometimes forget that, simply on the basis of the vision, courage and skill of such young men, this country was carrying the greatest freight air load in the world. That was not per capita. We were carrying the greatest air freight load in the world before the second world war. That was achieved because groups of young men organized air routes, and with the competitive spirit of vigorous young Canadians showed what could be done in the uncharted routes of the great north as well as the charted routes of the south. It'is a glorious page in the development of Canadian aviation. Then the second world war came and once again this country demonstrated the peculiar qualities possessed by its people. Young men and young women again showed that Canada has special qualifications to lead the world in civil aviation. In this country the commonwealth air training* plan not only brought together many thousands of young people from every part of the commonwealth to take their training together but also produced as a necessary part of that training an unusually large number of airports all through the country. Many of those airports are still available for uses to which they are not now being put.
In 1945 we ended the war with a tremendous reservoir of trained men and women ready to take their part in the extension of our air services. We had airports and buildings dotted all over the country in the smaller

as well as the larger communities. Since that time many of these young men and women have been able to carry forward their training in civilian life. Because of that background Trans-Canada Air Lines has been able to establish a safety record second to none anywhere in the world. In addition there are other air services in this country which have also given the quality and kind of service that we would expect would be given by young men and women of the type trained here.
Having said that, one must say with a sense of realism that we have not gone nearly as far as we should have with the opportunities we possessed. We have a great trunk route across Canada. We have certain routes north and south. We have certain routes connecting the larger Canadian cities with cities in the United States. But if you look at a map showing the air lines in this country you will see that we have neither the number of routes we should have in Canada on trunk services, nor those feeder lines that we should have all over this country making use of those smaller airports, and some very large airports, which were built during the war in smaller communities.

I rise to a point of order. When the hon. gentleman commenced his speech I did not take objection because I thought he was going to deal with the administration item. However, he has gone on for almost fifteen minutes to deal with the Aeronautics Act, which I had hoped I might bring in this afternoon, and with Trans-Canada Air Lines. I repeat to the committee that I have no responsibility for Trans-Canada Air Lines, and I say now I know of no vote in the main estimates that deals with Trans-Canada Air Lines. It is true that some of the statements made by the hon. gentleman in reference to air policy generally would come under the administration item; but I am sure he does not want to enter into a discussion of the Aeronautics Act at this time, nor does he want to enter upon a full discussion of Trans-Canada Air Lines, because I do not think that would be fair either to the committee or to me. So, Mr. Chairman, I ask you to apply the rules.

I submit that I am completely within the rules and that this is the time to bring forward the proposals I have been making and others I had intended to make. It will not take me very long to complete what I have to say. However, this simply demonstrates the very difficulty I am seeking to emphasize, a difficulty that can be overcome by the government. Item 499 under the Department of Transport deals with civil aviation, including the administration of the
Supply-Transport
Aeronautics Act and regulations issued thereunder. The very next item has to do with airways and airports.

That is exactly the point I am making, that those are the items on which the hon. gentleman should make his speech; and he should make his speech, I suggest, without discussing the Aeronautics Act under a general administration item such as this.

I had not thought there was any doubt but that under the general item of administration it was the established practice and very well settled rule that one could discuss any of the items that must be administered by the minister whose department we are considering. Let us see why that is such a sound proposition. The item under discussion deals with departmental administration, which embraces every item under this department. Consequently, if we want to discuss a subject that touches more than one item the appropriate place to discuss that subject is on the opening item of administration, which necessarily deals with every other item in the estimates of that department.
I wanted to point out that I was not dealing with Trans-Canada Air Lines alone, nor with the new Aeronautics Act. I was dealing with the act for which provision is made in these estimates, and was seeking to point out why I hoped that before we finish these estimates, and before we come to a consideration of the amendments to the Aeronautics Act, the government will take a very simple step it can take and transfer Trans-Canada Air Lines to the administration of this department so that we will be able to discuss the whole subject at that time. That is why I was bringing up this matter this evening.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman has completed his remarks?

No; the chairman rose. I did not intend to speak very much longer, but I do submit that I am entirely within the rules. I had hoped to be helpful so that my suggestions, if they were worthy of consideration, could be given that consideration over the week end in order that when we resumed our discussion the government might make its decision with respect to them.

I have no doubt the suggestions are worthy of consideration; far be it from me to say otherwise; but I do not think this is the place to discuss them. If I may say so respectfully, I entirely disagree with the hon. gentleman in the interpretation he places upon the departmental administration item. This is an item which permits the discussion of matters concerning the

Supply-Transport
Department of Transport generally. The other, particular, items permit the discus-ion of those things to which they relate. My hon. friend has been discussing Trans-Canada Air Lines, which do not come under any item in the estimates. He has been discussing in detail the Aeronautics Act, which I submit with deference should not be discussed on the general item but on the two items to which he referred, and which will be up for consideration when the amendments are brought in. I do submit, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. gentleman is out of order.

Well, I am not going to take any unnecessary time in arguing the point.
I believe I am entirely in order. I sought to place before the committee reasons why these matters should be given consideration, but rather than continue any argument about it I shall wait until the items come up, though I believe that will involve more time and do away with the possibility of bringing the whole operation into the position I think . would be best in the interests of civil aviation. I would point out that I was not discussing any single item of Trans-Canada Air Lines, or any single item under the act. I was discussing the broad problem of civil aviation and the desirability of bringing it under one all-embracing organization, in the interests of the expansion of the services we need in this country. If the minister argues against a discussion of that kind at this time, however, rather than argue as to who is right and who is wrong in the interpretation of the rules I shall defer my discussion until we come to the items, though it will only lengthen the time necessary for discussion.

On this item last year the hon. member for Cumberland .and I brought up the question of restoring ferry service across Minas Basin between Parrsboro on the one side and Kingsport and Wolfville on the other. At that time the minister said a suitable boat could not be had, or something of that kind. As he knows, that ferry service was carried on for many years, and was done away with during the war. I believe it is some 175 miles around the bay if you have to go by car, and if you are in a hurry that is a long way to drive. I wonder if the minister has given any consideration to the restoration of this ferry service in the near future. I am sure it would be of great interest to many people in Nova Scotia.
I am not in a position to give the hon. gentleman the information he desires now. This is a matter which concerns the maritime commission, and when we come to that item I will have the information.

On March 8 and again on March 22 of this year I broached the subject

of railways and trucking. If my memory serves me aright, on those occasions the minister said he would be willing to discuss that matter more fully when his estimates came up. I am not sure of the appropriate place to discuss that question. If the minister thinks it would not be appropriate under this item and will tell me the proper place in his estimates, I shall refrain from any further comment. Otherwise I want to go on and discuss the demand of the railways before the royal commission and any other body they can get to listen to them that some control be imposed upon trucking in Canada.
I would appreciate it if my hon. friend could postpone the discussion of that subject until we get to one of the Canadian National railway items.
Would the minister indicate to me the particular item? I should be glad to do that to accommodate the minister.
I shall indicate it in a moment. I think perhaps the most appropriate item would be the board of transport commissioners.
On what page is that?
Page 64, item 524.

Of course, the minister
realizes the difficulty of those of us who are on other committees. When that item is reached, there may be-
I do not want to stop the hon. member from discussing it, and if he should not be in the house when this item is discussed I shall indicate an appropriate item under which he can discuss it.
I want to thank the minister for that.

I should like to ask the minister a question arising out of the control of airports. From the markings on them, I judge that the Department of Transport controls the airports. Presumably the department controls the landing, taking off, storage of planes, taxiing and all the other operations around the airport. Where is the division of authority between the Department of Transport and Trans-Canada Air Lines? Naturally each airport has a control tower, and in the control tower there is an officer in charge of telling aircraft whether they can land. I think it is important for the committee tc have a statement as to where one jurisdiction ends and the other begins. Trans-Canada Air Lines is in charge of the aircraft. Is that company in charge of the aircraft once it is off the ground, or under whose authority is the plane operating when it comes in to land?

It seems to me that if there are two authorities there is possibility of duplication and unnecessary operational expenses.

I do not think there is any difference between the operations of the airport in so far as Trans-Canada Air Lines are concerned and any other air line. The hon. member seems to think there is a distinction to be made between Trans-Canada and the other air lines, in so far as the arrival or departure at the airport is concerned, but there is not. I presume the airplane is in constant communication with the control tower if it is flying on the beam. If it has left the beam, then it is in communication I presume with other landmarks, so that it can steer its course appropriately. I do not think there is any distinction to be drawn. There is no duplication, because there is no service performed by the air line which is again performed by the control tower.

I asked the question because I gather that most airports are used by more than one air line. At the appropriate time, or perhaps now, will the minister state how the Department of Transport is paid for the operation of the airport? Is it on a per plane basis, on a rental basis, a per passenger basis or how?

The department is not paid for the operation of the airport. Moneys are voted in these estimates that are now before the house for the operation and maintenance of airports. There are some exceptions to that, in that a municipality may own an airport. The department does charge landing fees and the like, which are paid by the air lines to the department.

In the Vancouver press a day or two ago, there was a statement to the effect that the department was going to extend the runways at the international airport. Some action of that kind is needed in order to satisfactorily accommodate the transpacific planes. I believe they are having some difficulty there now because of the size of the runways. Will the minister say what the position is with regard to any such proposal?
I would rather do so when we reach the particular item.
Move the airport to Abbotsford.

Another question has to do with the regulations for safety at sea. When the minister made his statement concerning fire regulations on April 21, he mentioned that he was adapting them from the safety at sea regulations, which were agreed upon at the convention in London in 1948. Is it the plan to adopt all those regulations which
Supply-Transport
were agreed upon at London, and will those regulations include some provision to force ships on the coast to carry a radio operator?
There has been a great deal of discussion on that point. Last fall there was a wreck on the shores of Stanley park within the city of Vancouver, and the radio telephone was not in operation.
The accident to which my hon. friend refers was not due to a lack of radio apparatus.
Will the new regulations provide for the carrying of radio operators on those ships?

I was asked that question by the member for Vancouver East some days ago. I am afraid I shall have to give the same answer as I gave to him. It is impossible to give that information until the bill is before the house. It has been announced that the bill will be introduced in the near future. It is not ready at the moment, but I hope it will be ready soon. When the bill is before the house, there will be ample opportunity for discussion. I should not like to anticipate any information by giving it now.

When the minister's estimates come up again, I hope he will give the committee a detailed statement concerning the benefits that may be obtained by the men of the merchant navy. So far as I know, the only improvement in their position since last session has been some extension of their right to vocational training. They still have no right whatever to educational training, pensions, hospitalization benefits, the Veterans Land Act benefits, civil service preference or any of the other benefits which are available to the men of the other services. Will the minister be prepared to make a statement on their position at the present time?
Yes, I shall make a statement.

I hope he will say why those benefits are only available to the men who signed a pool contract. Apparently quite a few men were taken on at such a young age that they could not sign a contract with the manning pools and other men were taken on to Canadian ships without ever being asked to sign a manning pool contract. Yet for some reason or other both these groups are ineligible for vocational training. Will the minister also deal with that situation when he brings in his report?
I said I would give a statement.

The minister will cover that in the statement?

Supply-Transport
I am not saying that I will cover that. I said that I will make a statement. The hon. gentleman is asking so many questions-
I have not asked many questions. Do not get excited.

We have had a discussion on this time and again, and I know what my hon. friend's views and feelings are. If my friend gets one concession, he will ask for ten. I told him that I would give a statement. Now he says "Will the minister introduce this matter in the statement?" What else does the hon. member want?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Pipe lines.

I should like to see the minister get this item through by eleven o'clock, but there is something I want him to clarify. This is not only a matter of administration. I think it is a matter of change of policy. I am going to use that Sydney airport as an example. I think the Department of Transport owns that airport. You have the Dutch airlines planes landing there, and those of the American airlines; and there are planes from all over the world coming in. Since the inception of the port, under the minister's department, the cleaning and ramp service and all of that work which is of a labour nature was performed by local people and employees of the T.C.A. Within the last year or so there is moving in there an organization known as Allied Aviation Services, and they are taking over or attempting to take over the servicing of planes that are not Trans-Canada Air Lines planes.
I wrote to the minister giving him the whole story. I have before me a letter dated April 29 of this year. I do not as a rule read back letters to anyone in the house on a matter on which they have made a decision. But I think in this particular letter the minister is absolutely wrong. I know that he did not write the letter, that he obtained the information from his officials and that they relayed it to him. In this letter he makes the statement:
There is nothing we can do about the situation existing in Sydney.
About which I had written him. The letter continues:
As you know, Allied Aviation Services is a Canadian company, even though it may have American affiliations and backing and we cannot very well prevent them from soliciting business at Sydney or anywhere else.
It is my interpretation of that statement and it is my information that that particular
organization is an American company; and in view of the fact that the airport belongs to the Department of Transport, I think it is the responsibility of that department to see that the servicing of ships coming into that port, their property, should be done by either members of the T.C.A. or the Department of Transport. Definitely, it should be Canadian labour.
I am merely bringing this matter back to the minister's attention so that he may have another look at it with his officials. I have been out to the port and have discussed this matter with the employees. If you let that American company muscle in there, it means that you are going to displace practically everyone who is performing that service at that airport at this time, and most of them are veterans of the recent war and have been there for some considerable time. I wish' the minister would have another look at the situation and I hope that, some time before his estimates are finished, he will be in a position to tell me exactly what he thinks the situation is. I do not think this letter answers the question.
I shall be glad to take another look at it.

Item agreed to.
